title: Pirates of the Scumribbean - Pirate Borg review (Solo RPG Friday)
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jdAA_65-h0E

Daniel (@dungeondive) reviews *Pirate Borg*, and it lands as far more than a re-theme of Mork Borg — it reads, he argues, like Mork Borg with several supplements baked into the core book. Fresh off a session GM'd by Paul of Stone Axe Tabletop Gaming, he walks the volume: the dark Caribbean's alternate history, the undead rising, and Ash, a drug rendered from undead flesh.

Mechanically it is familiar — d20 against a target of twelve, the players rolling everything — with meaningful additions. Spirit is split out from Presence as a fifth ability governing willpower, relics and spellcasting, a change he would happily port back into Mork Borg. The apocalypse becomes a d66 story-and-chapter table to mine for adventures rather than an inevitability, and Devil's Luck lets you cheat fate outright. Classes run Brute to Zealot, plus Haunted Souls who return undead and Tall Tales who arrive as mermaids or sentient animals.

The big addition is naval combat: ships with their own stats, crews to be manned and paid, broadsides, shanties, wind and foul weather, up to ghost ships and vessels from the deep. Add generators for derelicts, treasure maps and uncharted islands, plus the Curse of Skeleton Point sandbox, and he calls it unreservedly great.

----

*Pirate Borg* splits spellcasting off Presence into a new Spirit stat, and Daniel likes it enough to want it back-ported into Mork Borg. Does a fifth stat sharpen a rules-light game, or is that the first step away from what made it light?
